speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: asked the Prime Minister whether he can (i) list all the components of the salaries of the Ministers and Prime Minister, (ii) state the amounts, in months of salary, paid for each component for each year from 2013 to 2017 and (iii) confirm that these components are fully included in the Ministerial salary benchmark established in the White Paper on "Salaries for a Capable and Committed Government" that was debated in Parliament in January 2012 and are not payments over and above the salary benchmark.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Committee had received more than 500 emails and letters from Members of Parliament and the public, including young people, Chief Executive Officers, small and medium enterprise (SME) owners, retirees, overseas Singaporeans, professionals, academics, as well as representatives from non-government organisations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee set out to first determine what the appropriate level of total annual salary should be.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee then recommended how this total amount should be divided between fixed pay and variable pay.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The fixed pay comprises the monthly salary and 13th month Non-Pensionable Annual Allowance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee recommended that a significant part of the total annual salary should be variable, and the quantum linked to individual performance and national outcomes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The variable components of the annual salary comprise individual Performance Bonus, National Bonus and the Annual Variable Component.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And, together, these variable components constitute 35% of the total norm annual pay, and this is quite usual for executives and senior people at this level.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The fixed pay is 65% of total norm annual pay.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There are no hidden salary components or perks.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Prime Minister’s salary does not have an individual Performance Bonus as there is no individual who can assess his performance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But to keep to the principle of making a significant part of the Prime Minister’s total pay subject to performance, that is, 35%, the Prime Minister’s variable pay has twice the National Bonus compared to other Ministers, linking it to national outcomes, in place of the individual Performance Bonus.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Again, this includes all components, including his National Bonus, and there are no salary components or perks beyond this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have prepared a handout on the range and average of each of the variable pay components received by Political Office Holders over the past five years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If Members can refer to the handout, (Annex 1) reflects the actual variable pay components received by Political Office Holders over the past five years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: All these variable components are in accordance with the framework I earlier described, and not on top of it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The bonuses can be higher than the norm in the framework, or lower, depending on the actual performance of individual Political Office Holders and the national outcomes in each year.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The National Bonus is determined equally by the four national indicators laid out in the White Paper, namely, the real median income growth rate of Singaporeans; the real growth rate of the lowest 20th percentile income of Singaporeans; the unemployment rate of Singaporeans; and the real gross domestic product growth rate.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Annual Variable Component is always the same amount that all Civil Servants receive.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Performance Bonus is determined by the Prime Minister who consults the senior Ministers in Cabinet in assessing the performance of Political Office Holders.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In determining the Performance Bonus for each individual, he takes into account the actual work that each Political Office Holder does in the specific responsibilities assigned to him, as well as his contributions in Cabinet when we consider broader national issues.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Many Political Office Holders hold more than one portfolio, in order to stretch them and to build depth and experience in the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I should emphasise that each Office Holder receives only one salary regardless of whether he holds one or multiple portfolios.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Emeritus Senior Minister Goh Chok Tong is not a member of the Cabinet, and has not received a ministerial salary since he retired from the Cabinet in May 2011.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The 2012 White Paper on "Salaries for a Capable and Committed Government" was submitted by an independent Committee after extensive consultation with Members of Parliament and the public.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The paper was endorsed in full in January 2012, after a thorough debate in this House over two and a half days with 29 Members speaking on the matter, including seven Members from the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In determining the salary framework, the Committee was guided by the following three key principles.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, salaries must be competitive so that people of the right calibre are not deterred from stepping forward to lead the country.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, the ethos of political service entails making sacrifices and, hence, there should be a discount of 40% in the pay formula.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, there should be a "clean wage" with no hidden perks.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Members of Parliament, including those from the Workers’ Party, endorsed these principles.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I quote Mr Chen Show Mao – he is in the House, "We (the Workers' Party) agree with the three principles that political salaries should be competitive, that political service is a calling that has its own ethos and their wages should be transparent." During that Parliamentary session, the Workers' Party had proposed their own formula based on these same principles.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Handout 2 (Annex 2) is a Straits Times report on the 2012 debate in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The handout provides a succinct summary of the key points and conveys a flavour of the debate.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It reports that there was, I quote, "Real progress in   ministerial pay debate", and quoting my remarks that the "Opposition’s agreement on key points marks a breakthrough", and the "Shift in the Workers' Party's stance helps debate move forward".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This would have made the link between salary and performance weaker, though both the WP's and the White Paper’s proposals would have added up to the same norm annual salary.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the Committee of Supply (COS) debate this year, I informed this House that the Prime Minister had formed a new independent Committee in 2017 to review the salary framework to ensure that it remains appropriate and valid.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The 2017 Committee reaffirmed the three key principles and was of the view that the current salary structure for Political Office Holders remained relevant and sound.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Significantly, no member of the Opposition sought clarification on my COS statement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Leon Perera has also filed a similar Parliamentary Question for Written Answer on Ministerial Salaries, which I believe Table 1 in my handout answers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Before I proceed to the concluding segment of my reply, with your permission, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to invite Members, in particular Mr Perera, to seek any clarifications that they may have.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One, since the revision in 2012, in percentage terms, has the average income of our Ministers increased or decreased?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Of course, it can go up and it can go down, depending on whether the National Outcomes were achieved and the individual performance of the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there are no hidden perks, no hidden medical benefits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister stated that the three components of Mr Alex Yam's question had been answered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second part actually requests the Prime Minister to state the amounts in months of salary paid for the year from 2013 to 2017.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What we have in the first handout is a range in the number of months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Do we have details on the absolute dollar amount that was requested in the Parliamentary Question (PQ) by Mr Alex Yam?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I should point out that Mr Leon Perera asked the question for a Written Answer and his question was fully answered in the written form.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Had Mr Leon Perera chosen to ask an Oral question, he could have expanded, he could have asked, but he chose not to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I invite him to ask any questions for clarifications that he may have.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And, of course, Mr Pritam Singh as well, who was present during the debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would that not have been an opportunity to, at that point, when the written PQ was answered, and also disclose and publish the National Bonus level, in addition to the Performance Bonus level, which I think was the point that Mr Pritam Singh was making?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question is: would the Government be publishing the quantums of National Bonus and average highest and lowest Performance Bonus on an annual basis, going forward?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, if that was what Mr Leon Perera wanted, he could have filed an Oral question and he could have followed up, and we would have provided him the answer, as we would today.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I am answering all the questions today.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But could I ask Mr Perera whether he agrees that Ministers' salaries should be competitive, that the salary should recognise the ethos of public service and that salaries should be transparent, which was the Workers' Party's position in 2012?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My PQ did not raise a suggestion with relation to the salary, the formulation for calculating the total compensation of the salary, and I have no disagreement with those broad principles, in response to the Deputy Prime Minister's question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would also like to pose a question in relation to my original Written question filed in September.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It was in relation to total Bonus Months.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I would like to ask the hon Deputy Prime Minister: has the figure for the National Bonus – which I acknowledge is the same for all Ministers – been previously published prior to when the Written question was filed in September?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: All the factors are there and it can be calculated.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I think people have made an attempt to do so; not very far off from where it actually was.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I take it that Mr Leon Perera does affirm that he agrees that Ministerial salary should be competitive, that the salary should recognise the ethos of public service and that salaries should be transparent.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Can I ask Mr Perera whether he agrees that the salary proposals that the Workers' Party had put forward in 2012 would essentially result in the same total annual salaries for Ministers as the White Paper, except for the Workers' Party's proposal having a much larger component of fixed pay?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For the Deputy Prime Minister's question, I was not present in the House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I did not participate in this debate and, in my PQ, I did not make a suggestion or a new suggestion about how the total compensation or the monthly salary should be calculated.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have provided him all the information there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think with the assumption that this information is descriptive in nature, then, clearly, there are no grounds for me to disagree that it is a description of what had been presented during the debate in 2012 which I did not participate in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There is one point which I have to make, which is an important distinction even though the result is similar, is the basis upon which the monthly component is calculated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The principle that the Workers' Party took upon itself was to consider what would be a fair multiple, what sort of message do you send to the public with regard to appropriate salary that ultimately is derived.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We chose MX9 as the point, because we felt that an entry-level Civil Servant would aspire to that position, and he would not have to be a scholar or anything of that sort.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is our political perspective at that time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Government's perspective is to take the 1,000 top earners and then you take a percentage of their total salary and then give a discount of 40% or something of that nature.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the total amount, as it is accurately in the table, is correct.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second point I would like to suggest – and this is not belabouring the issue, Mr Speaker – is the question again by Mr Alex Yam about the amount.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe, in the context of the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods that came out with a list of recommendations, it is actually more propitious for us to present all the information in an easy-to-understand manner for the public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that would reduce the prospect of misinformation online.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand there is an issue with regard to Performance Bonus.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It does not need to specify what each Minister gets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I would like to read Recommendation 9 which would be a helpful way for the Government to move forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: They should ensure that they communicate with the public in clear and comprehensible terms." I do understand that "Factually", the Government website, put out a response to certain misinformation that was generated by Mr Leon Perera's question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: His question came out on 10 September; on 11 September, certain websites got carried away with certain information or the way they interpreted that reply.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I mean, Mr Perera asked for some data.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And the next day, the data was misinterpreted and became the widespread basis for false information.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am delighted that Mr Pritam Singh and the Workers' Party are all for transparency and for debunking falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, in 2012, there was remarkable convergence in this House on the matter of Ministers' salaries.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Pritam Singh has just said that the Workers' Party agrees with the principles underlying the current salary structure and that the Workers' Party's alternative formula used a norm salary level that is also $1.1 million.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The proposals, Mr Speaker, Sir, are really very close to each other – in principle and in quantum.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, Mr Speaker, Sir, if there were a Workers' Party government in power today, by their own formula, the Workers' Party Minister would be paid essentially the same as what a Minister today is paid.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Pritam Singh would pay himself that same amount.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The subject of Ministers' salaries, Mr Speaker, Sir, is a difficult one to talk about.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Even knowledgeable, well-meaning people, who have a deep interest in politics are susceptible to this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I read Mr Ho Kwon Ping's extensive interview with Channel NewsAsia, which was published yesterday.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Among other things, he suggested pegging Ministerial salaries to the median salary of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He also suggested an independent Commission to decide the actual quantum.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And Mr Louis Ng, in an earlier similar interview, also suggested that there should be public consultations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The independent Committee did have extensive consultations in 2012 and a significant part of Ministers' salaries are pegged not just to the growth of average salaries, but to the lowest 20th percentile of salaries and to the unemployment rate – issues which are important to every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But even Mr Ho, who is well-informed and has a deep interest in politics, has some serious misconceptions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He claimed, for example, that his salary is lower than the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Because, Sir, we need a fair, open, honest, transparent framework in place, so that we can continue to have able, committed and passionate people, with integrity, come to serve as our political leaders.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: My most important task now is to help Prime Minister Lee to prepare, not just the Fourth Generation leadership, but also to make sure that we are able to have a Fifth Generation of leaders coming in, having the time to learn, to be tested, and to gain the trust and support of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These are people in their late 30s and 40s.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Many would be at the threshold, where they have a good chance of reaching the peak in their chosen careers and professions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The PAP looks for people with integrity, who are capable, committed and caring, who are prepared to put others before themselves.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: All Members of this House know that coming into politics entails many sacrifices, in privacy, continuous exposure to the glare of the public eye in their careers, in family time, not always being there to watch your kids grow.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They are fair-minded people who have the interest of Singapore and Singaporeans at heart.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They have recommended a framework and a quantum that reflects all these things that we talk about – sacrifice, commitment to service, working for the good of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Workers' Party accepts the principles and has come up with essentially the same quantum, which Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Leon Perera just affirmed.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is what politics is about also – not just opposing for the sake of opposing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is a matter which, whether one is in the opposition or in government, we can agree upon – that we need a fair framework to bring in the best team, to do the best for Singapore and Singaporeans.
